title: Episode 250: Sacagawea: The Shoshone Guide, the Continental Traverse, and the Golden Dollar
description:
The extraordinary life and enduring legacy of Sacagawea: the young Lemhi Shoshone teenager who was captured in childhood, sold into marriage, and accompanied the Lewis and Clark Expedition across eight thousand miles of uncharted wilderness. Carrying her infant son Jean Baptiste on her cradleboard, Sacagawea rescued the expedition's priceless scientific journals from a capsized pirogue, recognized landmark geographic monuments, and orchestrated the miraculous reunion with her brother Chief Cameahwait that secured the pack horses needed to cross the Rocky Mountains. Discover the courage, botanical brilliance, and immortal story of the woman who helped guide America to the Pacific.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series honors one of the most remarkable women in world history: a teenage mother who carried her newborn child across eight thousand miles of mountain wilderness, bridging cultures and saving the Corps of Discovery. Here is George with the life of Sacagawea.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: CHILD OF THE SHOSHONE: KIDNAPPING AND SURVIVAL: 1788 TO 1804
Born around 1788 into the Agaidika or 'Salmon Eater' band of the Lemhi Shoshone nation in the rugged Salmon River country of modern Idaho, the girl who would become world-famous as Sacagawea was raised in a migratory mountain culture intimately attuned to the seasonal cycles of the Rocky Mountains. Her people harvested wild roots, fished mountain rivers, and ventured east into the Great Plains to hunt buffalo. Around age twelve, during a buffalo hunting expedition near the Three Forks of the Missouri, a war party of Hidatsa raiders attacked her camp, capturing young Sacagawea and taking her hundreds of miles east to their fortified earth-lodge villages on the knife-edge bluffs of the Missouri River in North Dakota. Living as an adopted captive among the Hidatsa, she learned their language and agricultural methods while retaining her fluent native Shoshone tongue. Around 1804, she was purchased or won in gambling as a second wife by Toussaint Charbonneau, a French-Canadian fur trader living among the Mandan. When Captains Meriwether Lewis and William Clark arrived in November 1804 to build their winter quarters at Fort Mandan, they quickly recognized that this sixteen-year-old Shoshone teenager held the geographical key to reaching the Pacific Ocean, as her native people controlled the only horses capable of crossing the formidable Rocky Mountains. In the Lemhi valleys of her early childhood, Sacagawea learned the delicate ecological rhythms of the northern Rockies, mastering the identification of edible roots, medicinal herbs, and seasonal game trails. Her Lemhi Shoshone name, translated poetically as 'Bird Woman' or 'Boat Launcher', carried the ancient memory of mountain streams and avian migrations across the northern Rockies.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BIRTH OF POMPEY AND THE DEPARTURE INTO THE UNKNOWN: FEBRUARY 1805
In early February 1805, inside the freezing wooden quarters of Fort Mandan, sixteen-year-old Sacagawea went into a prolonged, agonizing labor with her first child. Alarmed by her suffering, Lewis administered a traditional frontier remedy suggested by French voyageur René Jusseaume: crushing two rings of a rattlesnake's rattle into a cup of warm water. Within ten minutes, Sacagawea safely gave birth to a healthy baby boy, named Jean Baptiste Charbonneau. Captain William Clark was instantly enchanted by the infant, affectionately nicknaming him 'Pompey' or 'Pomp', forming a tender paternal affection that lasted for the rest of Clark's life. On April 7, 1805, when the Corps of Discovery launched their wooden pirogues into the Missouri River to push westward into terra incognita, Sacagawea strapped two-month-old Jean Baptiste onto a willow-framed cradleboard on her back. While eastern historical legends often romanticized her as an official paid guide holding compasses and maps, her true historical contribution was far more profound: she was an indispensable cultural interpreter, botanical expert, and living symbol of peace whose presence transformed thirty armed soldiers into an unthreatening diplomatic mission in the eyes of every native nation they encountered. Carrying two-month-old Jean Baptiste in a beaded willow cradleboard, Sacagawea endured swarms of mosquitoes, drenching rainstorms, and freezing winds with an unflinching quiet strength that earned the profound respect of every frontiersman in the party. Clark noted in his journal with deep affection that the presence of the infant Pompey brought warmth, laughter, and human gentle feeling into what was otherwise an exhausting, militaristic overland campaign.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE WHITE PIROGUE DISASTER: THE SAVING OF THE JOURNALS
On May 14, 1805, along the upper Missouri River in Montana, a sudden, violent squall struck the expedition's white pirogue, which was carrying Lewis and Clark's most precious scientific cargo: their navigational instruments, medicine chests, gunpowder reserves, and original handwritten field journals. Her husband Charbonneau was at the rudder and panicked in terror, freezing up and crying out to God while the pirogue tipped onto its side, filling with water and washing loose papers and specimens into the churning river. While the men shouted in panic, Sacagawea displayed extraordinary presence of mind and courage. Balancing calmly in the half-submerged boat with her infant son clutched in one arm, she reached over the gunwales into the icy water, catching and retrieving almost all of the floating books, navigational charts, medicine boxes, and irreplaceable manuscripts before they sank into the muddy current. Lewis was so deeply moved by her bravery and composure that when the expedition discovered a beautiful mountain tributary days later, they named it Sacagawea River in her honor, recording in their journals that she had saved the scientific record of the entire expedition. When the white pirogue capsized in the churning waves of the Missouri, Sacagawea acted with instinctive courage, securing the expedition's compasses, quadrant, and botanical notebooks while the frantic boatmen struggled to right the vessel. Lewis recorded his profound gratitude in his private diary, observing that Sacagawea had preserved the very foundation of the expedition's geographic and botanical legacy from watery oblivion.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE BOTANICAL LIFELINE AND THE BEAVERHEAD LANDMARK
As the expedition pushed deeper into the arid plains and mountain foothills of Montana, wild game became scarce and the men suffered from gastrointestinal illnesses and physical exhaustion. Sacagawea served as the expedition's nutritional savior: relying on her childhood botanical knowledge, she walked the riverbanks with a sharpened digging stick, unearthing nutritious wild prairie turnips, wild licorice, fennel, and artichoke tubers stored in underground vole caches. In late July 1805, as the Missouri split into three distinct rivers—named the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin—the expedition entered the mountainous realm of Sacagawea's childhood. On August 8, Sacagawea pointed to a striking rocky promontory towering over the Beaverhead River, excitedly informing Clark that her people called it 'The Beaver's Head' because it resembled a swimming beaver, and that they were now in the summer hunting grounds of her brother's band. Her landmark recognition gave the exhausted, doubting explorers renewed hope, confirming that they were on the correct trail to the Continental Divide. Sacagawea's unearthing of wild licorice, fennel, and prairie artichokes from underground rodent caches repeatedly rescued the expedition from severe scurvy and starvation during grueling weeks of scarce wild game. Her encyclopedic understanding of wild indigenous flora repeatedly proved the difference between health and scurvy, providing fresh greens and medicinal roots when game meat was scarce.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIRACULOUS REUNION AT LEMHI PASS: AUGUST 1805
On August 17, 1805, near modern Clark Canyon Reservoir in southwestern Montana, Clark and Sacagawea arrived at a council encampment where Lewis was attempting to negotiate with a band of Lemhi Shoshone horsemen. As Sacagawea entered the council lodge to interpret the proceedings, she stopped dead in her tracks, looked into the face of Chief Cameahwait, and let out an emotional cry of joy. Running forward, she threw her blanket over him and broke into passionate weeping: the chief was her own beloved brother! The council was transformed from a tense military negotiation into an emotional family reunion. Sacagawea's brother embraced his sister and her newborn infant, pledging his tribe's total friendship to the white explorers. The Shoshone supplied the expedition with twenty-nine strong pack horses, essential pack saddles, and an experienced guide to lead them over the terrifying granite passes of the Bitterroot Mountains. Without this providential family reunion, the Corps of Discovery would have been stranded on the eastern slopes of the Rockies with winter bearing down, facing certain starvation and disaster. The tearful embrace between Sacagawea and Chief Cameahwait stands among the most poignant moments in American history, turning a desperate geographical deadlock into a triumphant breakthrough across the Continental Divide. The sight of Sacagawea speaking directly to her brother in their ancestral tongue dissolved every barrier of fear, ensuring that the Shoshone gladly opened their horse herds to the American explorers.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: VOTING AT THE PACIFIC AND THE WHALE ON THE BEACH: 1805 TO 1806
Sacagawea's influence continued all the way to the Pacific Ocean. On November 24, 1805, when Lewis and Clark faced a critical decision on where to build their winter quarters along the Columbia River, they took a democratic vote of the entire party. In an astonishing break with nineteenth-century racial and gender conventions, Clark recorded Sacagawea's vote alongside those of the soldiers: 'Janey is in favor of a place where there is plenty of potatoes.' In January 1806, hearing that a massive blue whale had washed ashore on the Oregon coast near modern Cannon Beach, Sacagawea fiercely demanded that she be allowed to accompany the party to the ocean. She pointed out that she had traveled thousands of miles across mountains and rivers, yet had not been allowed to see the great water or the monstrous fish, insisting that it was unfair to leave her behind. Clark agreed, taking her to the beach, where she gazed with awe at the skeleton of the hundred-foot whale, purchasing three hundred pounds of blubber from local Tillamook villagers to provide oil for their winter camp. At Fort Clatsop, Sacagawea's vote to winter near the salt-producing ocean beaches reflected her practical frontier wisdom, ensuring that the men had access to vital sea salt to preserve meat for the eight-thousand-mile return trek. Her insistence on viewing the great ocean and the stranded whale demonstrated her fierce personal curiosity, refusing to be an invisible passenger in a historic journey across her native continent.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEGACY OF THE GOLDEN DOLLAR AND THE AMERICAN SPIRIT
In August 1806, when the returning expedition reached Fort Mandan, Charbonneau and Sacagawea remained behind. Captain William Clark was heartbroken to say goodbye, writing an emotional letter to Charbonneau offering to educate young Jean Baptiste in St. Louis as his own son: 'As to your little Son (my boy Pomp) you well know my fondness for him... if you are disposed to accept either of my offers to you and will bring him down, I will raise him as my own child.' Charbonneau accepted, and Clark oversaw Jean Baptiste's education in St. Louis, sending him to European courts where he became a fluent polyglot scholar. Sacagawea died tragically young in December 1812 at Fort Manuel in South Dakota at approximately age twenty-four, though Shoshone oral traditions maintain she returned to her people in Wyoming and lived to old age. In 2000, the United States Mint immortalized her memory on the golden Sacagawea dollar coin, depicting the young Shoshone mother looking over her shoulder with baby Jean Baptiste nestled on her back. Sacagawea remains an eternal symbol of indigenous courage, dignity, and maternal fortitude: the teenage girl whose quiet wisdom and unyielding spirit helped bridge two worlds and guide an infant republic across a continent. Sacagawea's image on the Golden Dollar coin forever celebrates her extraordinary role as an indigenous diplomat, loving mother, and continental pathfinder whose quiet bravery helped shape the destiny of North America. Her courage, dignity, and maternal love transcended the centuries, inspiring generations of Americans to revere the vital indigenous contributions that made the continental nation possible.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 251: Sitting Bull—Tatanka Iyotake, the Sun Dance Vision, the Little Bighorn, and the Standing Rock. Until then, stay curious.
